title: Compute-Efficient Personalisation of PPG Foundation Models
subtitle: How cheaply can a shared model be tuned to fit one person, when is that worth the cost, and does it help everyone equally?
question: How much predictive benefit does per-person adaptation of an open PPG foundation model provide over the per-person normalisation already standard in production, how much individual data does it require, and what does it cost at scale?
motivation: PPG foundation models are trained once for an entire population and do not change for an individual, so a model optimised for the average performs only moderately well for any particular person. Production systems address this through normalisation, scoring readings against a personal rolling baseline, which assumes the signal-to-outcome relationship is shared across people and only the centre and range differ. For some people the mapping itself differs, whether through vascular structure, arrhythmia, age, or the effect of skin tone on the optical signal, and only adapting the model can re-learn it. Whether that is worth doing is a question of compute allocation before it is one of accuracy.
methods: Heart-rate estimation on PPG-DaLiA, using the PaPaGei encoder in both its S and P variants. Six arms are compared on identical test sets: the population model, per-person normalisation, a warm-started per-person linear probe, parameter-efficient adaptation, full fine-tuning as an upper bound, and demographics as an optional cheap arm. Each is swept across adaptation budgets of 2 to 40 minutes and all-available data, under an activity-stratified split with a buffer between the adaptation and test blocks. Cost is measured primarily as trainable parameters per person, with stored bytes as the deployment translation.
